content: 1. The use of an innovative biometric system, eCompliance, has been explored for monitoring tuberculosis treatment in rural Uganda. This system aims to improve adherence to treatment protocols and ensure better patient outcomes. 2. An active defaulter tracing system was implemented in Kibera, Nairobi, Kenya, to enhance outcomes for HIV prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) and tuberculosis patients. This system focused on identifying and re-engaging patients who defaulted on their treatment. 3. Despite the presence of a retrieval system, a high rate of non-compliance with anti-tuberculosis treatment was observed in Saudi Arabia. This highlights the need for the implementation of directly observed therapy (DOT) to improve adherence. 4. A retrospective analysis of an electronic treatment adherence device piloted in the Northern Cape Province demonstrated its cost-effectiveness in improving tuberculosis treatment adherence. 5. In Chiang Rai, Thailand, women volunteers from higher socioeconomic backgrounds were engaged to support socioeconomically disadvantaged tuberculosis patients. This approach aimed to address disparities in treatment access and adherence. 6. In Shanghai, the incremental cost-effectiveness of improving treatment outcomes among migrant tuberculosis patients was evaluated. Financial and logistical interventions were found to enhance treatment success rates. 7. Transportation subsidies and living allowances were assessed for their impact on tuberculosis control outcomes among internal migrants in urban Shanghai, China. These measures were shown to improve treatment adherence and outcomes. 8. Financial incentives were provided to rural-to-urban tuberculosis migrants in Shanghai as part of an intervention study. This approach aimed to address economic barriers to treatment adherence. 9. In Brazil, food baskets were distributed to tuberculosis patients at a primary healthcare clinic. This intervention positively influenced treatment outcomes by addressing nutritional and economic challenges. 10. Ecuador’s national monetary incentive program was evaluated for its effects on adherence to treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis. The program demonstrated improvements in treatment adherence and outcomes. 11. A pay-for-performance system was implemented in Taiwan to control tuberculosis default cases and improve treatment adherence. This system incentivized healthcare providers to achieve better patient outcomes. 12. Financial incentives were used to improve adherence to tuberculosis treatment in a study conducted in the United States. This approach demonstrated effectiveness in enhancing treatment completion rates. 13. In Pakistan, a childhood tuberculosis desk guide and monitoring intervention were introduced to improve case management. This initiative aimed to standardize and enhance the quality of care for pediatric tuberculosis patients. 14. In Tomsk, Russia, alcohol treatment interventions were integrated into routine tuberculosis care. This approach addressed comorbid alcohol use disorders and improved overall treatment outcomes. 15. The cost and cost-effectiveness of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) treatment were analyzed in Estonia and Russia. The study highlighted the economic challenges and benefits of standardized treatment regimens. 16. In Peru, the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of standardized second-line drug treatment for chronic tuberculosis patients were evaluated. The study demonstrated the potential for scaling up such regimens in resource-limited settings. 17. A cohort study in the Philippines assessed the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. The findings supported the implementation of standardized treatment protocols. 18. A systematic review examined the cost and cost-effectiveness of treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. The review provided insights into optimizing resource allocation for MDR-TB management. 19. The End TB Strategy outlined global targets and strategies for tuberculosis prevention, care, and control beyond 2015. This comprehensive framework aimed to eliminate tuberculosis as a public health threat. 20. Community-based treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis was implemented in Khayelitsha, South Africa. This approach demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of decentralized care models. 21. Patient and program factors influencing default during treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were analyzed. The study identified key barriers to adherence and proposed strategies to address them. 22. A comparison of community-based care versus centralized hospitalization for MDR-TB patients was conducted in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The study highlighted the benefits of decentralized care in improving access and outcomes. 23. Cost-optimization strategies for treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were evaluated in Nigeria. The study emphasized the importance of efficient resource utilization in achieving better treatment outcomes. 24. The impact of reduced hospitalization on the cost of treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis was assessed in South Africa. Decentralized care models were found to be more cost-effective. 25. The treatment experience of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in Florida from 1994 to 1997 was documented. The study provided valuable insights into the challenges and successes of managing MDR-TB in a high-resource setting. 26. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined decentralized care for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. The findings supported the effectiveness of community-based care models in improving treatment outcomes. 27. The WHO policy on tuberculosis infection control in healthcare facilities, congregate settings, and households emphasized the importance of infection prevention measures to reduce transmission. 28. The efficacy and safety of levofloxacin for treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were evaluated in the Opti-Q study. This research contributed to optimizing treatment regimens for MDR-TB. 29. WHO consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment provided evidence-based recommendations for managing isoniazid-resistant and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. These guidelines emphasized individualized treatment regimens based on patient characteristics and drug susceptibility. 30. The use of bedaquiline and delamanid, alone or in combination, was examined for their role in treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. These novel agents offered new options for managing drug-resistant cases. 31. The effectiveness and safety of injectable agents used three times weekly versus daily were analyzed. This research aimed to optimize dosing schedules for better patient outcomes. 32. Group D3 agents, including p-aminosalicylic acid, carbapenems, and amoxicillin-clavulanate, were evaluated for their role in treating drug-resistant tuberculosis. These agents provided additional options for complex cases. 33. The WHO guidelines recommended longer regimens for managing multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, with durations of 18 months or more. These regimens aimed to achieve higher cure rates while minimizing adverse effects. 34. The impact of intensive-phase duration on treatment outcomes for MDR/RR-TB patients was assessed. Shorter and longer durations were compared to determine the optimal length for achieving successful outcomes. 35. The total duration of treatment for MDR/RR-TB patients was evaluated to determine whether shorter or longer regimens improved outcomes. This research informed the development of evidence-based treatment protocols.
